title: Quantifying the Impact of Technical Barriers to Trade
abstract: This book provides an up-to-date discussion of economic issues involved in analyzing regulations of product quality and performance in international trade. Among the issues addressed in this collection are restrictions on genetically modified foods and pesticide use and compatibility standards for computers. While such regulations may serve important goals, they may also interfere with international trade flow by raising the costs of compliance. This is of special concern to developing countries, which have found it difficult to meet the increasingly exacting regulations imposed by the United States and Europe.Keith E. Maskus and John S. Wilson gather prominent international trade specialists to ask whether the impacts of such regulations may be quantified systematically in order to inform the international policy debate. The essays included here cover all fronts of the debate over regulatory issues and trade conflicts. The discussion ranges from a review of how trade conflicts emerge and how they are managed by the international trading system to a technical analysis of the potential impact of European restraints on trade in genetically modified products to an examination of methods for estimating the costs of compliance with environmental regulations. Considerable attention is paid to whether the emergence and enforcement of stronger standards among developed economies could result in diminished trade opportunities for developing countries. At the same time, the possibility that standards could expand market access through resolving consumer information problems is analyzed.This book will appeal to international economists, international relations specialists, and individuals concerned about appropriate regulation of safety and health issues in the global economy.Keith E. Maskus is Professor of Economics, University of Colorado, Boulder. John S. Wilson is Lead Economist, Development Economics Research Group, The World Bank.

Full narrative

Quantifying the Impact of Technical Barriers to Trade by Keith Maskus, John Wilson and others was published by University of Michigan Press in 2001. It is part of the Studies in International Economics series. Conceptually, the work connects to International trade, Economic geography, Business, Geology and Economics.

OpenAlex records 153 citations. That places it in the top 10% of works in its field and year of publication. Citations peaked in 2009 with 32 citing works. Notable citing venues include Cambridge University Press eBooks, SSRN Electronic Journal and World Economy. The citing works include 79 journal articles, 36 book chapters, 18 preprints and 7 reports. They come from 27 countries, led by the United States, Switzerland and the United Kingdom.

It is recorded in 1 library collection. Its subject matter aligns with Partnerships for the goals among the Sustainable Development Goals.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

Keith Maskus and John Wilson’s Quantifying the Impact of Technical Barriers to Trade has become a clear reference point in international trade scholarship. With 153 OpenAlex citations, it sits in the top 10% of works for its field and year, and its influence is especially visible in later research on technical regulations, non-tariff measures, trade policy, and export quality. The book’s policy relevance is reinforced by its alignment with sustainability-oriented concerns and its sustained use across economics and trade-oriented research communities.

Full narrative

Published by University of Michigan Press in 2001 as part of the Studies in International Economics series, this book addressed a problem that has only grown more important: how product standards, quality regulations, and performance requirements shape international trade. Its focus on technical barriers to trade, including issues such as genetically modified foods, pesticide use, and computer compatibility standards, gave the work immediate relevance for both trade economics and policy debates.

The citation record shows durable scholarly uptake rather than a short-lived burst of attention. Citations accumulated steadily over time, and the book’s influence spans a wide range of publication types, led by journal articles but also including book chapters, preprints, reports, and dissertations. The citing literature is concentrated in international trade and economics, with strong links to World Trade Organization law, global trade and competitiveness, and development-related research. This pattern suggests that the book has served as a methodological and conceptual anchor for work examining how non-tariff measures affect market access and trade performance.

The venues and authors in the citing landscape further indicate broad disciplinary reach. Citations appear in specialist trade outlets as well as economics journals and policy-facing publications, and the geographic spread of citing work includes the United States, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Australia, China, South Korea, Malaysia, and Japan. The record also shows repeated engagement by authors working on technical regulations, environmental trade barriers, and export quality, which is consistent with the book’s role as a foundational source for later studies in these areas.

Evidence of community and teaching uptake is also present. Library holdings and subject classifications place the book squarely in international trade, non-tariff trade barriers, free trade, and consumer protection, indicating that it remains discoverable and relevant for study and reference. OpenAIRE records show repository presence, and the book’s inclusion in a major academic series further supports its continued visibility. Public-event data are unavailable in the record, so the most reliable story here comes from sustained scholarly citation and library reach.

Overall, Quantifying the Impact of Technical Barriers to Trade stands as an influential synthesis of trade regulation analysis whose impact is visible in later empirical and policy research. Its citation performance, top-decile standing, and continued resonance in trade, development, and sustainability-oriented debates show that it helped shape how scholars and policymakers think about the trade effects of standards and regulatory measures.
